2.17.54: But neither could Eurotas, nor the Po,
2.17.55: With poplar shaded, in one channel flew;
2.17.56: By diff'rent, and by distant banks they glide,
2.17.57: Are rivers both, but various in their tide.
2.17.58: There are more beauties, but there's none like thine,
2.17.59: There are more versed, but thou hast only mine;
2.17.60: No other charms can e'er inspire my muse,
2.17.61: And other themes I with disdain refuse.

2.18.1: While, Macer, you Achilles' choler sing,
2.18.2: And Greece before the walls of Ilium bring;
2.18.3: While feats of arms in Phrygian fields you tell,
2.18.4: And how old Tory by Grecion vengeance fell;
2.18.5: I my soft hours in softer songs employ,
2.18.6: And all my leisure give to love and joy.
2.18.7: When to high acts, my voice I strive to raise,
2.18.8: Love laughs at my attempt, and mocks my lays;
2.18.9: "Begone!" I often to my mistress cry,
2.18.10: But have not courage, yet, myself to fly.
2.18.11: Whene'er she sees me in this sullen fit,
2.18.12: She fondles me, and, on my knee will sit:
2.18.13: "Enough of this (say I), for shame give o'er,
2.18.14: Enough of love, we'll play the fool no more."
2.18.15: " Ah, is it then a shame to love?" she cries,
2.18.16: And chides, and melts me with her weeping eyes.
2.18.17: Around my neck her snowy arms she throws,
2.18.18: And to my lips with stifling kisses grows.
2.18.19: How can I all this tenderness refuse?
2.18.20: At once my wisdom, and my will I lose;
2.18.21: I'm conquer'd, and renounce the glorious train
2.18.22: Of arms, and war, to sing of love again:
2.18.23: My themes are acts, which I myself have done,
2.18.24: And my muse sings no battles but my own.
2.18.25: Once I confess I did the drama try,
2.18.26: And ventur'd with success on tragedy;
2.18.27: My genius with a moving scene agrees,
2.18.28: And if I ventured further I might please:
2.18.29: But love my heroics makes a jest,
2.18.30: And laughs to see me in my buskins drest.
2.18.31: Asham'd, and weary of this tragic whim,
2.18.32: For tender thoughts I quitted the sublime.
2.18.33: My mind my mistress bends another way,
2.18.34: Her must my muse in all her songs obey;
2.18.35: Though oft I do not what I write approve,
2.18.36: Like, or not like it, I must sing of love.
2.18.38: To great Ulysses I a letter frame,
2.18.39: Or for Oenone tender things indite,
2.18.40: Or soft complaints for injur'd Phillis write;
2.18.42: I sooth, or flatter Dido's fierce despair;
2.18.43: Whether I fan Medea's raging fire,
2.18.44: Or for sweet Sappho touch the Lesbian lyre;
2.18.45: Whether I Phaedra's lawless love relate,
2.18.46: Or Theseus' flight and Ariadne's fate:
2.18.47: Oh, that Sabinus, my departed friend,
2.18.48: Could from all quarters now his answers send!
2.18.49: Ulysses' hand should to his queen be known,
2.18.50: And wretched Phaedra hear from Theseus' son;
2.18.54: A sad reply, and Sappho cease to mourn:
2.18.55: Nor him whom she can ne'er possess, desire,
2.18.56: But give to Phoebus fane her votive lyre.
2.18.57: As much as you in lofty epics deal,
2.18.58: You, Macer, show that you love's passion feel,
2.18.59: And sensible of beauty's powerful charm,
2.18.60: You hear their call amid the noise of arms.
2.18.61: A place for Paris in your verse we find,
2.18.62: And Helen's to the young adult'rer kind;
2.18.63: There lovely Laodamia mourns her lord,
2.18.64: The first that fell by Hector's fatal sword.
2.18.65: If well I know you, and your mind can tell,
2.18.66: The theme's as grateful, and you like as well
2.18.67: To tune your lyre for Cupid as for Mars,
2.18.68: And Thracian combats change for Paphian wars;
2.18.69: If well I know you, and your works design
2.18.70: Your will, you often quit your camp for mine.

2.19.1: If for thyself thou wilt not watch thy whore,
2.19.2: Watch her for me that I may love her more.
2.19.3: What comes with ease we nauseously receive,
2.19.4: Who but a sot would scorn to love with leave?
2.19.5: With hopes and fears my flames are blown up higher;
2.19.6: Make me despair, and then I can desire.
2.19.7: Give me a jilt to tease my jealous mind;
2.19.8: Deceits are virtues in the female kind.
2.19.10: Play'd trick for trick, and kept herself still new;
2.19.11: She, that next night I might the sharper come,
2.19.12: Fell out with me, and sent me fasting home.
2.19.13: Or some pretence to lie alone would take;
2.19.14: Whene'er she pleas'd her head and teeth would ache:
2.19.15: Till having won me to the highest strain,
2.19.16: She took occasion to be sweet again.
2.19.17: With what a gust, ye gods, we then embrac'd!
2.19.18: How ev'ry kiss was dearer than the last!
2.19.19: Thou whom I now adore, be edified,
2.19.20: Take care that I may often be denied;
2.19.21: Forget the promis'd hour, or feign some fright,
2.19.22: Make me lie rough on bulks each other night.
2.19.23: These are the arts that best secure thy reign,
2.19.24: And this the food that must my fires maintain.
2.19.25: Gross easy love does, like gross diet, pall;
2.19.26: In squeasy stomachs honey turns to gall.
2.19.27: Had Danae not been kept in brazen tow'rs,
2.19.28: Jove had not thought her worth his golden show'rs:
2.19.29: When Juno to a cow turn'd Io's shape,
2.19.30: The watchman help'd her to a second leap.
2.19.31: Let him who loves an easy whetstone whore,
2.19.32: Pluck leaves from trees, and drink the common shore.
2.19.33: The jilting harlot strikes the surest blow,
2.19.34: A truth which I by sad experience know;
2.19.35: The kind, poor, constant creature we despise,
2.19.36: Man but pursues the quarry while it flies.
2.19.37: But thou dull husband of a wife too fair,
2.19.38: Stand on thy guard, and watch the precious ware;
2.19.39: If creaking doors, or barking dogs, thou hear,
2.19.40: Or windows scratch'd, suspect a rival there.
2.19.41: An orange wench would tempt thy wife abroad;
2.19.42: Kick her, for she's a letter-bearing bawd.
2.19.43: In short, be jealous as the devil in hell,
2.19.44: And set my wit on work to cheat thee well.
2.19.45: The sneaking city-cuckold is my foe;
2.19.46: I scorn to strike but when he wards the blow.
2.19.47: Look to thy hits and leave off thy conniving,
2.19.48: I'll be no drudge to any wittol living;
2.19.49: I have been patient, and forborne thee long,
2.19.50: In hope thou wouldst not pocket up thy wrong:
2.19.51: If no affront can rouse thee, understand
2.19.52: I'll take no more indulgence at thy hand.
2.19.53: What, ne'er to be forbid thy house and wife
2.19.54: Damn him who loves to lead so ill a life.
2.19.55: Now I can neither sigh, nor whine, nor pray;
2.19.56: All those occasions thou hast ta'en away.
2.19.57: Why art thou so incorrigibly civil?
2.19.58: Do somewhat I may wish thee at the devil
2.19.59: For shame, be no accomplice in my treason;
2.19.60: A pimping husband is too much in reason.
2.19.61: Once more wear horns, before I quite forsake her
2.19.62: In hopes whereof, I rest thy cuckold-maker.

3.1.1: Unhurt by steel, arose an ancient wood,
3.1.2: A mansion fit for some retiring god;
3.1.3: With craggy stones a secret grot was hung,
3.1.4: And in the midst a sacred fountain sprung;
3.1.5: The courting birds repeating songs of love,
3.1.6: With soft complainings sweetly fill'd the grove:
3.1.7: Here wand'ring thoughtful, and intent to choose
3.1.8: Some theme unsung, to please the busy muse;
3.1.9: Fair elegy came on with gentle pace,
3.1.10: Unforc'd her air and easy was her grace.
3.1.11: Her flaxen hair, in curious tresses wreath'd,
3.1.12: Ambrosial sweets and heav'nly odours breath'd;
3.1.13: A simple dress the careless charmer bore,
3.1.14: And loving looks, and smiles unartful wore.
3.1.15: Next came the goddess of the tragic scene,
3.1.16: With stately tread, and proud majestic mien
3.1.17: Her front severe, with hanging curls was drown'd,
3.1.18: Her length of robe was full, and swept the ground:
3.1.19: Her hand held out, a regal sceptre grac'd,
3.1.20: And Lydian buskins half her legs embrac'd.
3.1.21: She first; "Must love for ever tune thy voice,
3.1.22: Fond idle bard, and trifling in thy choice
3.1.23: Thy wanton songs employ the drunkard's tongue,
3.1.24: In ev'ry street thy ribald lays are sung;
3.1.25: The finger marks thee in thy passing by,
3.1.26: 'Behold, where goes the slave of love,' they cry.
3.1.27: Thy lewd exploits, thou profligate, are grown
3.1.28: The public theme, and talk of all the town;
3.1.29: Whilst unconcern'd, and lost to sense of shame,
3.1.30: Thou still runn'st on nor mind'st thy ruin'd fame.
3.1.31: Enough thou'st told the plaints of fond desire,
3.1.32: Now let a nobler inspiration fire;
3.1.33: Thy matter cramps thy genius, learn to find
3.1.34: A manly subject, and exert thy mind.
3.1.35: In songs for girls, fond toys, and idle play,
3.1.36: Thy muse has wanton'd all her hours away.
3.1.37: But youth at length has fill'd its measure up;
3.1.38: My friend, 'tis time to taste of t'other cup.
3.1.39: Now in my service let thy force be shown,
3.1.40: Assert my honour, and retrieve thy own;
3.1.41: Thy sprightly fancy, and inventive wit,
3.1.42: The lofty style of tragic scenes will fit."
3.1.43: She said; and proudly rising in her gait,
3.1.44: Thrice shook her tresses, and display'd her state.
3.1.45: With open look (nor was my sight beguil'd)
3.1.46: And joyous eyes her rival sweetly smil'd;
3.1.47: Sustain'd her hand a myrtle branch upright?
3.1.48: Or did my fancy form the charming sight?
3.1.50: And canst thou ne'er forego thy sullen pride?
3.1.51: I not compare my lowly lays to thine;
3.1.52: Too weak materials for the vast design.
3.1.53: The style unlabour'd, negligent the dress,
3.1.54: My verse is humbler, and my matter less.
3.1.55: Gay, wanton, soft, my business is to move,
3.1.56: With melting strains, the playful god of love.
3.1.57: Bereft of me, fair Venus wants her charms,
3.1.58: I help the goddess, and prepare her arms.
3.1.59: My luring art, and soothing lays prevail,
3.1.60: Where lofty port, and tragic buskins fail.
3.1.61: I more deserve, by making that my care,
3.1.62: Thy rigid pride allows not thee to bear:
3.1.63: By me, Corinna first was taught to try
3.1.64: Tobreak from prison, and deceive the spy;
3.1.65: I first induc'd the fearful fair to slide
3.1.66: With tremb'ling caution from her husband's side;
3.1.67: When to thy arms, all loose, and disarray'd,
3.1.68: Prepar'd for pleasure, flew the melting maid.
3.1.69: Fix'd on her door, how oft I've hung on high,
3.1.70: Expos'd, and patient of each gazing eye!
3.1.71: How oft, in secret, while the keeper stay'd,
3.1.72: Within her woman's panting bosom laid!
3.1.73: Once sent a birthday gift, the cruel dame
3.1.74: In pieces tore, and gave me to the flame.
3.1.75: I taught thee first to cultivate thy mind;
3.1.76: Thy fancy brightened, and thy wit refin'd;
3.1.77: Thou to my care those merits must allow,
3.1.78: For which my rival would seduce thee now;"
3.1.79: They spoke. I answer'd, "Let me both conjure
3.1.80: To spare a mind with terrors unsecure;
3.1.81: Nor to my charge, when once pronounc'd, be laid
3.1.82: As crimes, the words my trembling tongue has said.
3.1.83: To gain me glory, thy decrees ordain
3.1.84: The regal sceptre and the tragic strain;
3.1.85: With painful labour need I toil for fame,
3.1.86: When easier tasks already raise my name?
3.1.87: Thou mak'st my love immortal; thee I choose:
3.1.88: Be thou my queen, and still command my muse.
3.1.89: Majestic pow'r, forgive my simple choice,
3.1.90: Thy gentle rival has obtain'd my voice.
3.1.91: Short is the time in which her palm is won;
3.1.92: Ere thine is gain'd, the poet's life is done."
3.1.93: I lowly said: she gracious gave assent,
3.1.94: And diff'rent ways the parting rivals went.
3.1.95: Ye gentle loves, complete the work assign'd,
3.1.96: A greater labour seems to press behind.

3.2.1: Not in the Circus do I sit to view
3.2.2: The running horses, but to gaze on you;
3.2.3: Near you I choose an advantageous place,
3.2.4: And whilst your eyes are fix'd upon the race,
3.2.5: Mine are on you—Thus do we feast our sight,
3.2.6: Each alike pleas'd with objects of delight;
3.2.7: In softer whispers I my passion move,
3.2.8: You of the rider talk, but I of love.
3.2.9: When, to please you, I straight my subject quit
3.2.10: And change my wishes to your favourite;
3.2.11: Oh. might I ride, and be so much your care,
3.2.12: I'd start with courage from the barrier,
3.2.13: And with a swift short compass brush the goal—
3.2.14: Unless the sight of you my course restrains,
3.2.15: And makes my hands forego the loosen'd reins;
3.2.16: As Pelops gaz'd on Hippodamia's face,
3.2.17: Till he had almost lost th' important race;
3.2.18: Yet he his mistress by her favour won;
3.2.19: So may our prize assist us when we run.
3.2.20: "What mean these starts? you must not, can't remove:
3.2.21: This kind auspicious place was fram d for love.
3.2.22: I fear you're crowded,- Gentlemen, forbear,
3.2.23: Pray let your arms and knees the lady spare;
3.2.24: Madam, your gown hangs down-nay, pray let me—
3.2.25: Oh heav'ns! what fine, what curious legs I see!
3.2.26: Sure, who Diana in a forest drew,
3.2.27: Copied in this the graceful'st parts from you;
3.2.28: Such Atalant discovering as she ran,
3.2.30: I burn'd and rag'd before—what then are these,
3.2.31: But flames on flames, and waters to the seas?
3.2.32: By these a thousand other charms are guess'd,
3.2.34: Oh for some air! this scorching heat remove,
3.2.35: Your fan would do't, but 'tis the heat of love."
3.2.36: But now the pomp appears, the sacred throng
3.2.37: Command applauses from the heart and tongue;
3.2.38: First victory with expanded wings does move,
3.2.39: Be near, O Goddess! to assist my love;
3.2.40: To Mars let warriors acclamations raise,
3.2.41: The merchants' tongues resound with Neptune's praise;
3.2.42: Whilst I, whom neither seas nor arms invite,
3.2.43: In love alone, the fruit of peace, delight;
3.2.44: To their Apollo let the prophets pray,
3.2.45: And hunters to Diana homage pay.
3.2.46: Let the mechanics to Minerva vow,
3.2.47: Rustics to Ceres, and to Bacchus bow;
3.2.48: Whilst I devote myself to thee alone,
3.2.49: Kind Venus, and the pow'rful god thy son;
3.2.51: Inform with all thy softness these fair eyes,
3.2.52: And to love's cause her gentle breast incline;
3.2.53: She grants, and has contriv'd it with a sign;
3.2.54: Do you assure it too, you who're to me
3.2.56: By all these heavenly witnesses' to you
3.2.57: Will I be ever faithful, ever true.
3.2.58: Now ib the open cirque the game's begun,
3.2.59: The praetor gives the signal, now they run;
3.2.60: I see which way your wishes are inclin'd,
3.2.61: To him a certain conquest is design'd;
3.2.62: For e'en the horses seem to know your mind.
3.2.63: He takes too large a compass to come in,
3.2.64: And lets his adversary get between;
3.2.65: Recall him, Romans, for a second heat,
3.2.67: Now see your ground you better do maintain,
3.2.68: This lady's favour, and your fame regain;
3.2.69: The prize is his.-As yours successful prove,
3.2.70: So let my wishes, which are all for love;
3.2.71: I'm yet to conquer, and your heart's the prize;
3.2.72: Something she promis'd with her sparkling eyes,
3.2.73: And smil'd;-" Enough," did I transported cry,

3.3.1: Can there be gods?-has she not falsely swore?
3.3.2: Yet is the beauty that she was before!
3.3.3: The curious tresses of her dangling hair,
3.3.4: As long, and graceful still as e'er they were;
3.3.5: That same inimitable white and red,
3.3.6: Which o'er her face was so distinctly spread,
3.3.7: The roses, and the lilies keep their place,
3.3.8: And ev'ry feature still as justly grace;
3.3.9: Her sparkling eyes their lustre still retain,
3.3.10: That form, that perfect shape does still remain,
3.3.11: As if she ne'er had sinn'd; and heav'n, ('tis plain)
3.3.12: Suff'ring the fairer sex to break their vows,
3.3.13: To the superior pow'r of beauty bows.
3.3.14: T' inforce my credit to her perjuries,
3.3.15: Oft would she swear by those persuasive eyes;
3.3.16: As if that charm had been too weak to move,
3.3.17: Sh'as added mine;-tell me, ye pow'rs above,
3.3.18: Why all this pain? why are these guiltless eyes
3.3.19: For her offence th' atoning sacrifice?
3.3.20: Was't not enough Andromeda has died,
3.3.21: An expiation for her mother's pride?
3.3.22: Is't not enough, that unconcern'd you see
3.3.23: (Vain witnesses for truth, for faith, for me,)
3.3.24: Such an affront put on divinity,
3.3.25: Yet no revenge the daring crime pursue,
3.3.26: But the deceiv'd must be her victim too?
3.3.27: Either the gods are empty notions, crept
3.3.28: Into the minds of sleepers as they slept,
3.3.29: In vain are fear'd, are but the tricks of law,
3.3.30: To keep the foolish cred'lous world in awe;
3.3.31: Or, if there be a god, he loves the fair,
3.3.32: And all things at their sole disposal are.
3.3.33: For us are all the instruments of war
3.3.34: Design'd, the sword of Mars, and Pallas' spear;
3.3.35: 'Gainst us alone Apollo's bows are bent,
3.3.36: And at our hands Jove's brandish'd thunder sent.
3.3.37: Yet of the ladies, oh! how fond are they!
3.3.38: Dare not the inj'ries they receive, repay,
3.3.39: But those who ought to fear them they obey.
3.3.40: Jove to his votaries is most severe;
3.3.41: Temples nor altars does his lightning spare.
3.3.43: But those who merit, can escape the fires.
3.3.44: Is this the justice of your pow'rs divine?
3.3.45: Who then will offer incense at a shrine?
3.3.46: Why do we thus reproach the deities?
3.3.47: Have they not hearts?-and surely they have eyes,
3.3.48: Nay, had I been a god, I had believ'd
3.3.49: The lovely criminals, and been deceiv'd;
3.3.50: Had wav'd the judgments to their perj'ries due,
3.3.51: And sworn myself that all they spoke was true.
3.3.52: Since then the gods such ample gifts bestow,
3.3.53: As make you absolute o'er men below;
3.3.54: Pray let me find some mercy in your reign,
3.3.55: Or spare at least your lover's eyes from pain.

3.4.1: Vex not thyself and her, vain man, since all
3.4.2: By their own vice or virtue stand or fall.
3.4.3: She's truly chaste, and worthy of that name,
3.4.4: Who hates the ill, as well as fears the shame;
3.4.5: And that vile woman whom restraint keeps in,
3.4.6: Tho' she forbear the act, has done the sin.
3.4.7: Spies, locks, and bolts may keep her brutal part,
3.4.8: But thou'rt an odious cuckold in her heart.
3.4.9: They that have freedom use it least, and so
3.4.10: The power of ill does the design overthrow.
3.4.11: Provoke not vice by a too harsh restraint;
3.4.12: Sick men long most to drink, who know they mayn't.
3.4.13: The fiery courser, whom no art can stay,
3.4.14: Or rugged force, does oft fair means obey;
3.4.15: And he that did the rudest arm disdain,
3.4.16: Submits with quiet to the looser rein.
3.4.17: A hundred eyes had Argus, yet the while
3.4.18: One silly maid did all those eyes beguile;
3.4.19: Danae, tho' shut within a brazen tow'r,
3.4.20: Felt the male virtue of the golden show'r;
3.4.21: But chaste Penelope, left to her own will
3.4.22: And free disposal, never thought of ill;
3.4.23: She to her absent lord preserv'd her truth,
3.4.24: For all th' addresses of the smoother youth,
3.4.25: What's rarely seen, our fancy magnifies;
3.4.26: Permitted pleasure who does not despise?
3.4.27: Thy care provokes beyond her face, and more
3.4.28: Men strive to make tho cuckold than the whore.
3.4.29: They're wondrous charms we think, and long to know
3.4.30: That in a wife enchants a husband so:
3.4.31: Rage, swear, and curse, no matter, she alone
3.4.32: Pleases, who sighs, and cries, " I am undone."
3.4.33: But could thy spies say, " We have kept her chaste,"
3.4.34: Good servants then, but an ill wife thou hast;
3.4.35: Who fears to be a cuckold is a clown,
3.4.36: Not worthy to partake of this lewd town,
3.4.37: Where it is monstrous to be fair and chaste,
3.4.38: And not one inch of either sex lies waste.
3.4.39: Wouldst thou be happy? with her ways comply,
3.4.40: And in her case lay points of honour by:
3.4.41: The friendship she begins, wisely improve,
3.4.42: And a fair wife gets one a world of love:
3.4.43: So shalt thou welcome be to ev'ry treat,
3.4.44: Live high, not pay, and never run in debt.

3.5.1: 'Twas in the midst and silent dead of night,
3.5.2: When heavy sleep oppos'd my weary sight,
3.5.3: This vision did my troubled mind affright:-
3.5.4: To Sol expos'd there stood a rising ground,
3.5.5: Which cast beneath a spacious shade around;
3.5.6: A gloomy grove of spreading oaks below,
3.5.7: And various birds were perch'd on ev'ry bough;
3.5.8: Just on the margin of a verdant mead,
3.5.9: Where murm'ring brooks refreshing waters spread
3.5.10: To shun the heat I sought this cool recess,
3.5.11: But in this shade I felt my heat no less;
3.5.12: When browzing o'er the flow'ry grass appear'd
3.5.13: A lovely cow, the fairest of the herd.
3.5.14: By spotless white distinguished from the rest,
3.5.15: Whiter than milk from her own udder press'd;
3.5.16: Whiter than falling, or the driven snow,
3.5.17: Before descending mists can make it flow.
3.5.18: She, with a lusty bull, her happy mate,
3.5.19: Delighted, on the tender herbage sat;
3.5.20: There, as he crops the flow'rs, and chews the cud,
3.5.21: Feasting a second time upon his food,
3.5.22: His limbs with sudden heaviness oppress'd,
3.5.23: He bends his head, and sinks to pleasing rest.
3.5.24: A noisy crow, cleaving the liquid air,
3.5.25: Thrice with lewd bill pick'd off the heifer's hair;
3.5.26: The glossy white imbib'd a spreading blot,
3.5.27: But on her breast appear'd a livid spot.
3.5.28: The cow rose slowly from her consort's side,
3.5.29: But when afar the grazing bull she spied,
3.5.30: Frisk'd to the herd, with an impetuous haste,
3.5.31: And pleas'd, in new luxuriant soil, her taste.
3.5.33: What may this visionary dream portend,
3.5.34: If dreams in any future truth can end?
3.5.35: The prophet nicely weighs what I relate,
3.5.36: And thus denounces in the voice of fate:-
3.5.37: "That heat you tried to shun i' th' shady grove,
3.5.38: But shunn'd in vain, was the fierce heat of love.
3.5.39: The cow denotes the nymph, your only care,
3.5.40: (For white's th' expressive image of the fair,)
3.5.41: And you the bull, abandon'd to despair.
3.5.42: The picking crow some busy bawd implies,
3.5.43: Who with base arts will soon seduce your prim.
3.5.44: You saw the cow to fresher pasture range,
3.5.45: So will your nymph for richer lovers change;
3.5.46: As mixing with the herd you saw her rove,
3.5.47: So will the fair pursue promiscuous love;
3.5.48: Soon will you find a foul incestuous blot,
3.5.49: As on the cow you view'd the livid spot."
3.5.50: At this my blood retired, with dismal fright,
3.5.51: And left me pale as death; my fainting sight
3.5.52: Was quite o'ercast in dusky shades of night.

3.6.1: Thy course, thy noble course a while forbear,
3.6.2: I am in haste now going to my dear!
3.6.3: Thy banks how rich, thy stream how worthy praise
3.6.4: Alas, my haste! sweet river, let me pass.
3.6.5: No bridges here, no ferry, not an oar,
3.6.6: Or rope to haul me to the farther shore!
3.6.7: I have remember'd thee a little one,
3.6.8: Who now with all this flood com'st blund'ring down.
3.6.9: Did I refuse my sleep, my wine, my friend,
3.6.10: To spur along, and must I here attend?
3.6.11: No art to help me to my journey's end!
3.6.12: Ye Lapland powers, make me so far a witch,
3.6.13: I may astride get over on a switch.
3.6.14: Or, for some griffin, or that flying horse,
3.6.15: Or any monster to assist my course;
3.6.16: I wish his art that mounted to the moon,
3.6.17: In shorter journey would my job be done.
3.6.18: Why rave I for what crack-brain'd bards devise,
3.6.19: Or name their lewd unconscionable lies?
3.6.20: Good river, let me find thy courtesy,
3.6.21: Keep within bounds, and mayst thou ne'er be dry.
3.6.22: Thou canst not think it such a mighty boast,
3.6.23: A torrent has a gentle lover cross'd.
3.6.24: Rivers should rather take the lover's side,
3.6.25: Rivers themselves love's wondrous power have tried.
3.6.26: 'Twas on this score Inachus, pale and wan,
3.6.27: Sickly and green, into the ocean ran;
3.6.28: Long before Troy the ten-years siege did fear,
3.6.29: Thou, Xanthus, thou Neaera's chains didst wear;
3.6.30: Ask Achelous who his horns did drub,
3.6.31: Straight he complains of Hercules's club.
3.6.33: Was then contested such outrageous fray!
3.6.34: It neither was for gold, nor yet for fee;
3.6.35: Dejanira, it was all for thee.
3.6.36: E'en Nile so rich, that rolls thro' sev'n wide doors,
3.6.37: And uppish over all his country scours,
3.6.38: For Asop's daughter did such flame contract,
3.6.39: As not by all that stock of water slack'd.
3.6.40: I might a hundred goodly rivers name,
3.6.41: But must not pass by thee, immortal Thame;
3.6.42: Ere thou couldst Isis to thy bosom take.
3.6.43: How didst thou wind and wander for her sake!
3.6.44: The lusty — with broad Humber strove;
3.6.45: Was it for fame? I say it was for love.
3.6.46: What makes the noble Ouse up from the main
3.6.47: With hideous roar come bristling back again?
3.6.48: He thinks his dearest Dervent left behind,
3.6.49: Or fears her false, in new embraces joined.
3.6.50: Thee also some small girl has warm'd, we guess,
3.6.51: Tho' woods and forests now hide thy soft place.
3.6.52: Whilst this I speak, it swells and broader grows,
3.6.53: And o'er the highest banks impetuous flows.
3.6.54: Dog-flood, what art to me? or why dost check
3.6.55: Our mutual joys? and, churl, my journey break?
3.6.56: What wouldst, if thee indeed some noble race,
3.6.57: Or high descent, and glorious name did grace?
3.6.58: When of no ancient house or certain seat,
3.6.59: (Nor, known before this time, untimely, great)
3.6.60: Rais'd by some sudden thaw thus high and proud,
3.6.61: No holding thee, ill-manner'd upstart flood;
3.6.62: Not my love-tales can make thee stay thy course,
3.6.63: Thou—zounds, thou art a—river for a horse.
3.6.64: Thou hadst no fountain, but from bears wert pist,
3.6.65: From snows, and thaws, or Scotch unsav'ry mist.
3.6.66: Thou crawl'st along, in winter foul and poor,
3.6.67: In summer puddled like a common-shore.
3.6.68: In all thy days when didst a courtesy?
3.6.69: Dry traveller ne'er laid a lip to thee.
3.6.70: The bane to cattle, to the meadows worse,
3.6.71: For something all, I for my sufferings curse.
3.6.72: To such unworthy wretch, how am I sham'd,
3.6.73: That I the gen'rous am'rous river nam'd!
3.6.74: When Nile and Achelous I display'd,
3.6.75: And Thame and Ouse, what worm was in my head
3.6.76: For thy reward, discourteous river, I
3.6.77: Wish, be the summers hot, the winters dry.

3.7.1: Was she not heavenly fair, and rich attir'd?
3.7.2: Was she not that which all my soul desir'd?
3.7.3: Yet were these arms around her idly spread,
3.7.4: And with an useless load I press'd the bed.
3.7.5: E'en to my wishes was the power denied,
3.7.6: When with my wishes the kind nymph complied
3.7.7: I lay without life's animated spring,
3.7.8: A dull, enervate, worthless, lumpish thing.
3.7.9: My neck she folded with a soft embrace,
3.7.10: Now kissed my eyes, now wanton'd o'er my face,
3.7.11: Now lov'd to dart her humid tongue to mine,
3.7.12: Now would her pliant limbs around me twine,
3.7.13: And sooth, by thousand ways, the sweet design.
3.7.14: The moving blandishments of sound she tried,
3.7.15: And, " My dear life, my soul, my all," she cried.
3.7.16: In vain, alas! the nerves are slacken'd still,
3.7.17: And I prov'd only potent in my will;
3.7.18: A poor inactive sign of man I made,
3.7.19: And might as well for use have been a shade.
3.7.20: If old I live, how shall I old prevail,
3.7.21: When in my youth I thus inglorious fail?
3.7.22: The bloom of years becomes my shameful moan,
3.7.23: Now in full growth the ripen'd man is shown,
3.7.24: But not the strength of man to her was known.
3.7.25: Untouched by brothers, sisters thus retire,
3.7.26: Or vestals rise to watch th' eternal fire;
3.7.27: Yet many a nymph whom I forbear to name,
3.7.28: Rave kindly yielded, and indulg'd my flame
3.7.29: Nor could the vigour of their 0vid blame.
3.7.30: Corinna knows when numb'ring the delight,
3.7.31: Not less than nine full transports crown'd the night.
3.7.32: Is verse or herbs the source of present harms?
3.7.33: Am I a captive to Thessalian charms?
3.7.34: Has some enchantress this confusion brought,
3.7.35: And in soft wax my tortur'd image wrought
3.7.36: Deep in the liver is the needle fix'd?
3.7.37: Plagues she by numbers, or by juices mix'd?
3.7.38: By numbers sudden the ripe harvest die,
3.7.39: And fruitful urns no more their streams supply;
3.7.40: Oaks shed, unshook, their acorns at the call,
3.7.41: And the vine wonders why her clusters fall.
3.7.42: Why may not magic act on me the same,
3.7.43: Unstring the nerves, and quite untune the frame!
3.7.44: Gall'd at the heart, and longing to perform,
3.7.45: I rais'd indeed, but rais'd an empty storm;
3.7.46: Most disappointed when the most propense,
3.7.47: And shame was second cause of impotence.
3.7.48: What limbs I touch'd! and only touch'd! oh, fie!
3.7.49: Where was the blissful touch? her shift can vie
3.7.50: In feasts like these, and touch as well as I.
3.7.51: Yet to touch her e'en Nestor might grow young,
3.7.52: And centuries, like twenty-one, be strung.
3.7.53: Such was the maid; the parallel had ran
3.7.54: Graceful, if I could add, such was the man.
3.7.55: Some envious deity with vengeance glow'd,
3.7.56: So sweet a gift had been so ill bestow'd.
3.7.57: I burn to clasp her naked in my arms,
3.7.58: Did she not freely open all her charms?
3.7.59: What boots good fortune, if we want the pow'r
3.7.60: To snatch the pleasures of the favour'd hour?
3.7.61: I, like a miser, only could behold,
3.7.62: And brooded o'er an useless mine of gold;
3.7.63: So Tantalus with fruit untouch'd is curst,
3.7.64: And dies amid the gliding stream of thirst;
3.7.65: So rises early from th' untasted fair,
3.7.66: The grave old prelate, and kneels down to pray'r,
3.7.67: Were yet her melting kisses misenploy'd?
3.7.68: Did she strive vainly to be well enjoy'd?
3.7.69: Sure she has beauties might deaf rocks enchant,
3.7.70: Bend the proud oak, and soften adamant;
3.7.71: She would have mov'd a man tho' almost dead,
3.7.72: But with my manhood the whole life was fled.
3.7.73: If none should lend an ear, why is the song,
3.7.74: Or painted nymphs shown to a blinded throng!
3.7.75: Ye gods! what joys did not my fancy raise!
3.7.76: I curl'd in folds of love a thousand ways.
3.7.77: Strong were my thoughts, but ah! my body lay
3.7.78: Languid as roses pluck'd off yesterday.
3.7.79: Now all the blood the circling spirits fire,
3.7.80: And the lost field impertinent require;
3.7.81: Begone untimely nerves! I trust no more,
3.7.82: Such was the promise of your strength before.
3.7.83: Could you the fair one balk of her delight,
3.7.84: Disgrace your master by so base a fright,
3.7.85: And want the courage for so sweet a fight?
3.7.86: Did she not kindly too your stay demand,
3.7.87: And tempt it softly with a soothing hand?
3.7.88: But when solicitings no life could gain,
3.7.89: And inspirations, tho' from her, were vain;
3.7.90: "Who bade thee thus thyself to me to bring!
3.7.91: Go for a silly unperforming thing:
3.7.92: Art thou a wretch by some curs'd spell destroy'd,
3.7.93: Or here com'st fribbling with past pleasure cloy'd?"
3.7.94: She spoke, and springing from the bed she flew,
3.7.95: And secret beauties so disclos'd to view;
3.7.96: Yet to conceal the joyless night's digrace,
3.7.97: She called for water with a smiling face,
3.7.98: And wash'd a nameless unpolluted place.

3.8.1: What coxcomb will in future times think fit
3.8.2: To build in love his fortune on his wit?
3.8.3: Wealth now is worth, whatever 'twas of old,
3.8.4: And merit valu'd by its weight in gold.
3.8.5: With male and female, this is now the rule,
3.8.6: And he that's poor, of course must be a fool.
3.8.7: The dame to read my am'rous verse delights,
3.8.8: My writings likes, but scorns the man that writes;
3.8.9: They freely on her privacy presume,
3.8.10: And find admittance where I must not come;
3.8.11: Me when she does her haunted house exclude,
3.8.12: To them she's civil, as to me she's rude.
3.8.13: Me she exposes to a thousand harms,
3.8.14: To walk the streets, while they are in her arms.
3.8.15: For whom does she my passion disregard?
3.8.16: And who has intercepted my reward?
3.8.17: Why is the beau with so much joy embrac'd?
3.8.18: His pockets full, it seems, his coat is lac'd:
3.8.19: He won her with his military air
3.8.20: Which cheats as often as it charms the fair.
3.8.21: Could she her longing eyes forbear to fix
3.8.22: On his fine feather, and his coach and six!
3.8.23: Enrich'd by plunder, he could never miss
3.8.24: The favour, who would buy the venal bliss.
3.8.25: No matter how he got his wealth, by war,
3.8.26: And blood: she cares not, if she has her share.
3.8.27: The upstart forward was, 'tis said, in fight,
3.8.28: And in the field of battle made a knight:
3.8.29: But had his honour come without his gold,
3.8.30: His, sure, had been like my reception, cold.
3.8.31: To men of merit how could she be coy,
3.8.32: Yet to a murd'rer prostitute the joy?
3.8.33: That head which lolls upon your panting breast,
3.8.34: Was lately cover'd with a plumy crest.
3.8.35: Can you the bully to your bed admit?
3.8.36: Are his hard limbs for ladies' dalliance fit?
3.8.37: His hands in your embrace you'll find embru'd
3.8.38: With clotted, and perhaps with guiltless blood;
3.8.39: How awkward must it be for you to feel,
3.8.40: Near yours, his thigh that late was cas'd with steel
3.8.41: That ring, the token of his pride and state,
3.8.42: Was with a heavy gauntlet hid of late:
3.8.43: Canst thou have commerce with a thing so foul!
3.8.44: Where's now the boasted niceness of thy soul?
3.8.45: What pleasure canst thou in his roughness find?
3.8.46: Thou that wert once the softest of thy kind!
3.8.47: Behold what marks of brutal rage he bears,
3.8.48: And how he's mangled with dishonest scars.
3.8.49: Yet to these scars, dishonest as they are,
3.8.50: His wealth he owes, his fortunes with the fair.
3.8.51: No doubt, he makes a merit of his guilt,
3.8.52: And brags what blood he has in battle spilt.
3.8.53: Fine courtship this, to win a gentle dame;
3.8.54: Thou shar'st his money, and must share his shame.
3.8.55: Me, not the meanest of Apollo's train,
3.8.56: She hates, and I repeat my verse in vain;
3.8.57: I sing before her gate; her gate I find
3.8.58: Is less obdurate than her harden'd mind.
3.8.59: Forbear your songs, Apollo's sons, forbear,
3.8.60: And bend your future thoughts to arms and war.
3.8.62: To murder, and to rapine use your hands,
3.8.63: And you with ease reduce the female bands.
3.8.64: Had Homer in the Grecian army serv'd,
3.8.65: We ne'er had heard that he had begg'd, or starv'd.
3.8.66: Of gold the thund'rer show'd the mighty pow'r,
3.8.67: Descending softly thro' the brazen tow'r,
3.8.68: And clasping Danae in a golden show'r.
3.8.69: A thousand bars the virgin fair did hold,
3.8.70: But what are iron bars to bribes of gold?
3.8.71: Against this foe her father could not guard;
3.8.72: Watchmen, and women kept a fruitless ward.
3.8.73: The damsel, who herself before was coy,
3.8.74: Melts at the sight, and meets the dazzling joy.
3.8.75: When peaceful Saturn did heav'n's sceptre sway,
3.8.76: Deep in earth's womb the fatal metal lay;
3.8.77: None then their teeming mother's bowels tore,
3.8.78: In quest of hidden wealth, in various ore;
3.8.79: Fed with the fruits which bounteous nature yields,
3.8.80: In painted gardens, and in golden fields,
3.8.81: From her rich soil are reap'd spontaneous crops,
3.8.82: And from the forest oak sweet honey drops.
3.8.83: No hinds as yet did toil their time away,
3.8.84: Nor with keen clusters wound the parent clay:
3.8.85: As yet no landmark was by lab'rers set,
3.8.86: And none had learned to plough the sea as yet
3.8.87: None as yet knew the use of sails and oars,
3.8.88: Nor ventur'd voyages beyond their shores.
3.8.89: The wit of men the race of men destroys,
3.8.90: And all its pow'rs against itself employs.
3.8.91: How subtle's human nature to contrive
3.8.92: Its proper ruin, and itself deceive!
3.8.93: Why didst thou cities with high walls surround,
3.8.94: Why arms invent thy jarring sons to wound?
3.8.95: What quarrel hast thou with the sea, and why
3.8.96: Didst thou at first the pathless ocean try?
3.8.97: Cannot the land content thy restless pride?
3.8.98: Didst thou with Saturn's sons the whole divide,
3.8.99: Thou wouldst not with three worlds be satisfied.
3.8.100: 'Tis strange thy vast ambition did not fly
3.8.101: O'er earth, and sea, and air, and scale the sky;
3.8.102: That man did not aspire to be a god,
3.8.103: And tread the paths by Indian Bacchus trod,
3.8.104: To give his name to some distinguish'd star,
3.8.105: And be what Hercules and Caesar are.
3.8.106: Instead of yellow harvests, now we seek
3.8.107: For solid gold, and thro' earth's entrails break;
3.8.108: The wealth we thus acquire's the soldier's prey,
3.8.109: And dearly for the blood he spills we pay.
3.8.110: The courts deny admittance to the poor,
3.8.111: In vain the needy clients crowd the door;
3.8.112: The judges to the rich decree the cause,
3.8.113: And money only gives their force to laws.
3.8.114: 'Tis money makes the judge with looks severe
3.8.115: Insult the poor, and give the rich his ear;
3.8.116: 'Tis money buys the title, makes the knight,
3.8.117: And dignifies with quality the cit:
3.8.118: Let money do all this, and more; the bar
3.8.119: Let money govern, and direct the war.
3.8.120: Let peace, as money sets the terms, be made,
3.8.121: But let it not the rights of love invade.
3.8.122: Let us enjoy this privilege at least,
3.8.123: That if we must be poor, we may with love be bless'd:
3.8.124: For now-a-days there's not a dame in town
3.8.125: So coy, but if you've money she's your own.
3.8.126: What tho' her keeper may an Argus be?
3.8.127: Blind him with money, and he'll nothing see.
3.8.128: What though her husband should by chance be by?
3.8.129: He'll leave the house, let you your money fly.
3.8.130: If there's a god above, to whom belongs
3.8.131: The cause of love, and slighted lovers wrongs,
3.8.132: Revenge the false one's mercenary scorn,
3.8.133: And let ill-gotten pelf to dirt return.

3.9.1:
Stepney.
If Memnon's fate bewail'd with constant dew,
3.9.2: Does, with the day, his mother's grief renew,
3.9.3: If her son's death mov'd tender Thetis' mind
3.9.4: To swell with tears the waves, with sighs the wind;
3.9.5: Sad Cupid now despairs of conqu'ring hearts,
3.9.6: Throws by his empty quiver, breaks his darts:
3.9.7: Eases his useless bows from idle strings;
3.9.8: Nor flies, but humbly creeps with flagging wings.
3.9.9: He wants, of which he robb'd fond lovers, rest;
3.9.10: And wounds with furious hands his pensive breast.
3.9.11: Those graceful curls which wantonly did flow,
3.9.12: The whiter rivals of the falling snow,
3.9.13: Forget their beauty, and in discord lie,
3.9.14: Drunk with the fountain from his melting eye.
3.9.15: Nor Phoebus, nor the muses' queen, could give
3.9.16: Their son, their own prerogative, to live.
3.9.17: Orpheus, the heir of both his parents' skill,
3.9.18: Tam'd wond'ring beasts, not death's more cruel will.
3.9.19: Linus' sad strings on the dumb lute do lie.
3.9.20: In silence forc'd to let their master die.
3.9.21: His mother weeping does his eyelids close,
3.9.22: And on his urn, tears, her last gift, bestows.
3.9.23: His sister too, with hair dishevell'd, bears
3.9.24: Part of her mother's nature, and her tears.
3.9.25: With those, two fair, two mournful rivals come,
3.9.26: And add a greater triumph to his tomb:
3.9.27: Both hug his urn, both his lov'd ashes kiss,
3.9.28: And both contend which reap'd the greater bliss.
3.9.29: Thus Delia spoke (when sighs no more could last)
3.9.31: "When youth with vigour did for joy combine,
3.9.32: I was Tibullus' life, Tibullus mine;
3.9.33: 1 entertained his hot, his first desire,
3.9.34: And kept alive, till age, his active fire."
3.9.35: To her then Nemesis (when groans gave leave)
3.9.36: "As I alone was lov'd, alone I'll grieve;
3.9.37: Spare your vain tears, Tibullus' heart was mine,
3.9.38: About my neck his dying arms did twine:
3.9.39: I snatch'd his soul, which true to me did prove;
3.9.40: Age ended yours, death only stopp'd my love."
3.9.41: If any poor remains survive the flames,
3.9.42: Except thin shadows, and more empty names;
3.9.43: Free in Elysium shall Tibullus rove,
3.9.44: Nor fear a second death should cross his love.
3.9.45: There shall Catullus, crown'd with bays, impart
3.9.46: To his far dearer friend his open heart.
3.9.47: There Gallus (if fame's hundred tongues all lie)
3.9.48: Shall, free from censure, no more rashly die.
3.9.49: Such shall our poet's bless'd companions be,
3.9.50: And in their deaths, as in their lives, agree.
3.9.51: But thou, rich urn, obey my strict commands,
3.9.52: Guard thy great charge from sacrilegious hands.
3.9.53: Thou, earth, Tibullus' ashes gently use,
3.9.54: And be as soft and easy as his muse.

3.10.1: Now Ceres' feast is come, the trees are blown,
3.10.2: And my Corinna now must lie alone.
3.10.3: And why, good Ceres, must thy feast destroy
3.10.4: Man's chief delight, and why disturb his joy?
3.10.5: The world esteems you bountiful and good,
3.10.6: You led us from the field and from the wood,
3.10.7: And gave us fruitful corn, and wholesome food.
3.10.8: Till then poor wretched man on acorns fed;
3.10.9: Oaks gave him meat, and flow'ry fields a bed.
3.10.10: First Ceres made our wheat and barley grow,
3.10.11: And taught us how to plough, and how to mow;
3.10.12: Who then can think that she designs to prove
3.10.13: Our piety, by coldness in our love?
3.10.14: Or make poor lovers sigh, lament, and groan,
3.10.15: Or charge her votaries to lie alone?
3.10.16: For Ceres, though she loves the fruitful fields,
3.10.17: Yet sometimes feels the force of love, and yields:
3.10.18: This Crete can witness, (Crete not always lies)
3.10.19: Crete that nurs'd Jove, and heard his infant cries,
3.10.20: There he was suckled who now rules the skies.
3.10.21: That Jove his education there receiv'd,
3.10.22: Will raise her fame, and make her be believ'd;
3.10.23: Nay she herself will never strive to hide
3.10.24: Her love, 'tis too well known to be denied:
3.10.25: She saw young Jasius in the Cretan grove
3.10.26: Pursue the deer, she saw, and fell in love.
3.10.27: She then perceived when first she felt the fire,
3.10.28: On this side modesty, on that desire;
3.10.29: Desire prevail'd, and then the field grew dry,
3.10.30: The farmer lost his crop and knew not why;
3.10.31: When he had toil'd, manur'd his grounds, and plough' d,
3.10.32: Harrow'd his fields, and broke his clods, and sow'd,
3.10.33: No corn appear'd, none to reward his pain,
3.10.34: His labour and his wishes were in vain.
3.10.35: For Ceres wand'red in the woods and groves,
3.10.36: And often heard, and often told her loves:
3.10.37: Then Crete alone a fruitful summer knew,
3.10.38: Where'er the goddess came a harvest grew.
3.10.39: Ida was grey with corn, the furious boar
3.10.40: Grew fat with wheat, and wonder'd at the store:
3.10.41: The Cretans wish'd that such all years would prove,
3.10.42: They wish'd that Ceres would be long in love.
3.10.43: Well then, since then 'twas hard for you to lie
3.10.44: All night alone, why at your feast must I?
3.10.45: Why must I mourn, when you rejoice to know
3.10.46: Your daughter safe, and queen of all below?
3.10.47: 'Tis holy-day, and calls for wine and love;
3.10.48: Come, let's the height of mirth and humor prove,
3.10.49: These gifts will please our master pow'rs above.

3.11.1: So much I've suffer'd, and so long, no more
3.11.2: I'll bear the wrongs which I have borne before.
3.11.3: Begone, vile Cupid, I'll no more endure
3.11.4: Thy slavish labors, and fatigues impure;
3.11.5: From hence, I'll put an end to all the pains
3.11.6: Thou'st cost me, and from hence shake off thy chains.
3.11.7: I hate the liv'ry I with pleasure wore,
3.11.8: And blush at bonds, which once with pride I bore:
3.11.9: But this, methinks, should have been done before.
3.11.10: To leave my wicked courses I begin,
3.11.11: As years deprive me of the gust of sin.
3.11.12: On Cupid's neck I should have trod when young,
3.11.13: And vanquish'd him when my desires were strong.
3.11.14: In that there had been virtue; now there's none,
3.11.15: The world will say so; let the world say on.
3.11.16: Much opposition I shall meet; perhaps,
3.11.17: The lewd will laugh, and threaten a relapse.
3.11.18: To bear reproaches I must be prepar'd,
3.11.19: Easy's the end, when the beginning's hard;
3.11.20: Content let me the present pain endure,
3.11.21: For the sharp medicine is the patient's cure.
3.11.22: How oft you have expos'd me to the cold,
3.11.23: While in your arms you did my rival hold!
3.11.24: How like a slave have I been forc'd to wait
3.11.25: All weathers, and how oft have watched the gate!
3.11.26: As if your house was trusted to my care
3.11.27: And I, your sentinel, did duty there.
3.11.28: Oft have I seen your sated lover come
3.11.29: With looks, as if he long'd to be at home.
3.11.30: But what most grated on my jealous mind,
3.11.31: Was that he there the waiting fool should find.
3.11.32: That aggravated most the cruel curse;
3.11.33: I would not wish my greatest foe a worse.
3.11.34: How oft have I attended you abroad,
3.11.35: Or in the city, cirque, or on the road?
3.11.36: They took me for your husband by my care,
3.11.37: Or that your guardian or your slave I were.
3.11.38: I by the people's glances, and your own,
3.11.39: Observ'd you were acquainted with the town;
3.11.40: That of your love if I possess'd a part,
3.11.41: 'Twas plain I shared with many more your heart.
3.11.42: What need I of your perjuries bring proof,
3.11.43: Suppose the common talk was not enough!
3.11.44: What do your ogles and your gestures mean,
3.11.45: Your carriage at th' assembly and the scene?
3.11.46: There's scarce a fop you meet with in your way,
3.11.47: To whom you have not something soft to say;
3.11.48: Some token which you either understand
3.11.49: By mystic words or motion of the hand.
3.11.50: They tell me you are sick; I run to see,
3.11.51: And find, as ill as you pretend to be,
3.11.52: It is not for my rival, but for me.
3.11.53: I seldom told you of your faults, but strove
3.11.54: To cover all your failings with my love;
3.11.55: Of this I might remind you, and much more,
3.11.56: But what avails it now; th' affair is o'er:
3.11.57: A fond you found me, and a patient man,
3.11.58: And get you such another if you can.
3.11.59: I fear not now your frowns; my bark defies
3.11.60: The storm of words, and tempest of your eyes;
3.11.61: No coaxing now, your hardest phrases use,
3.11.62: Your looks, your language, all their terrors lose;
3.11.63: I am not such a fool as I have been,
3.11.64: To dread your spirit, and to sooth your spleen.
3.11.65: But, ah! by diff'rent passions I'm oppress'd,
3.11.66: Fierce love and hate contend within my breast;
3.11.67: My soul they thus divide, but love, I fear,
3.11.68: Will prove too strong, and get the mast'ry there;
3.11.69: I'll strive to hate her, but if that should prove
3.11.70: A fruitless strife, in spite of me I'll love.
3.11.71: The bull does not affect the yoke, but still
3.11.72: He bears the thing he hates against his will
3.11.73: I hate, I fly the faithless fair in vain,
3.11.74: Her beauty ever brings me back again;
3.11.75: She always in my heart will have a place,
3.11.76: I hate her humour, but I love her face;
3.11.77: No rest I to my tortur'd soul can give,
3.11.78: Nor with her nor without her can I live.
3.11.79: Oh! that thy mind we in thy face did view,
3.11.80: Less lovely that thou wert, or else more true.
3.11.81: How diffrent are thy manners and thy sight!
3.11.82: Thy deeds forbid us and thy eyes invite.
3.11.83: Thy actions shock us, and thy beauty moves,
3.11.84: And he who hates thy faults, thy person loves.
3.11.85: Happy, ah! ever happy should I be,
3.11.86: If I no charms or no defects could see.
3.11.87: Thee I conjure by all our past delights,
3.11.88: Our cheerful days and our transporting nights,
3.11.89: By all the imprecated gods above,
3.11.90: To whom thou art forsworn, but most by Love,
3.11.91: By thy fair face, which I as much adore
3.11.92: As all those gods, and own as much its pow'r,
3.11.93: Forgive me this offence, and I'll offend no more.
3.11.94: Be what thou wilt, thy humour good or ill,
3.11.95: I'll love thee, thou shalt be my mistress still
3.11.96: Ah, let my passion ever favour find,
3.11.97: Or be it with, or be't against my mind,
3.11.98: But rather let me sail before the wind.
3.11.99: Ah, let thy wishes with my will agree,
3.11.100: Since surely I thy slave must ever be;
3.11.101: In thee since I have centred all my joys,
3.11.102: Oh Venus! let my love be still my choice.

3.12.1: Ill-omen'd birds, how luckless was the day,
3.12.2: When o'er my love you did your wings display!
3.12.3: What wayward orb, what inauspicious star
3.12.4: Did then rule heav'n? what gods against me war?
3.12.5: She who so much my fatal passion wrongs,
3.12.6: Was known and first made famous by my songs.
3.12.7: I lov'd her first, and lov'd her then alone,
3.12.8: But now, I fear, I share her with the town.
3.12.9: Am I deceiv'd or can she be the same,
3.12.10: Who only to my verses owes her fame
3.12.11: My verse a price upon her beauty laid,
3.12.12: And by my praises she her market made;
3.12.13: Whom but myself can I with reason blame?
3.12.14: Without me she had never had a name.
3.12.15: Did I do this, who knew her soul so well?
3.12.16: Dearly to me she did her favours sell;
3.12.17: And when the wares were to the public known,
3.12.18: Why should I think she'd sell to me alone?
3.12.19: 'Twas I proclaim'd to all the town her charms,
3.12.20: And tempted cullies to her venal arms;
3.12.21: I made their way, I show'd them where to come,
3.12.22: And there is hardly now a rake in Rome
3.12.23: But knows her rates, and thanks my babbling muse:
3.12.24: Her house is now as common as the stews;
3.12.25: For this I'm to the muse oblig'd, and more
3.12.26: For all the mischiefs envy has in store.
3.12.27: This comes of gallantry, while some employ
3.12.28: Their talents on the fate of Thebes and Troy,
3.12.29: While others Caesar's godlike acts rehearse,
3.12.30: Corinna is the subject of my verse.
3.12.31: Oh, that I ne'er had known the art to please,
3.12.32: But written without genius and success.
3.12.33: Why did the town so readily believe
3.12.34: My verse, and why to songs such credit give?
3.12.35: Sure poetry s the same it ever was,
3.12.36: And poets ne'er for oracles did pass.
3.12.37: Why is such stress upon my writings laid?
3.12.38: Why such regard to what by me is said?
3.12.39: I wish the tales I've of Corinna told,
3.12.40: Had been receiv'd as fables were of old;
3.12.41: Of furious Scylla's horrid shape we read,
3.12.42: And how she scalp'd her hoary father's lead:
3.12.43: Of her fair face, and downward how she takes
3.12.44: The wolf's fierce form, the dog's, or curling snake's;
3.12.45: Serpents for hair, in ancient song we meet,
3.12.46: And man and horse with wings instead of feet.

3.13.1: My wife, a native of Phaliscan plains,
3.13.2: Where the rich soils enrich the lab'ring swains,
3.13.3: Where purple grapes and golden apples grow,
3.13.4: A conquest we to great Camillus owe.
3.13.5: When once to Juno's feast she thither went,
3.13.6: My mind to know the secret rites was bent:
3.13.7: The pious priests the solemn sports prepare,
3.13.8: And purify the fane with holy care.
3.13.9: A heifer of the place they sacrifice,
3.13.10: But ne'er to men expose their mysteries,
3.13.11: I mark'd the hidden way my consort went,
3.13.12: And follow'd down the deep and dark descent.
3.13.13: To an old wood at last I came, whose shade
3.13.14: Impress'd a horror on the gloom it made,
3.13.15: And ev'ry step with trembling feet I trod,
3.13.16: Profan'd, I thought, the dwelling of a god.
3.13.17: An altar there was rais'd by hands divine,
3.13.18: And fragrant incense flam'd around the shrine.
3.13.19: Chaste matrons there their vow'd oblations pay,
3.13.20: And celebrate with joyful hymns the day.
3.13.21: Soon as the fife the signal gives, they move
3.13.22: In long procession through the sacred grove
3.13.23: Branches and flow'rs are with devotion spread
3.13.24: O'er all the way, and priestly vestments laid.
3.13.25: Next after these, through loud acclaims, they lead
3.13.26: A cow milk white, and of Phaliscan breed;
3.13.27: Then a young steer, whose forehead ne'er had borne
3.13.28: The crooked honours of the butting horn.
3.13.29: The least of all the victims was a swine,
3.13.30: And then a ram whose horns around his temples twine.
3.13.31: A goat, whom most the goddess hates, comes last;
3.13.32: The present feels her vengeance for the past.
3.13.33: When in a wood to hide herself she tried,
3.13.34: She by the bleating of a goat was spied;
3.13.35: For this the beast is by the boys pursu'd;
3.13.36: For this she's ever greedy of its blood,
3.13.37: And he, who first the letcher wounds in play,
3.13.38: Claims by her law, and hears the prize away.
3.13.39: The tender youth, and tim'rous virgin strow
3.13.40: With robes the ground the goddess is to go.
3.13.41: The virgins' locks with golden fillets bound,
3.13.42: And sparkling diamonds glitt'ring all around;
3.13.43: Buskins embroider'd on their feet they wear,
3.13.44: And spreading trains with pride uneasy bear.
3.13.45: Here, as in Greece the custom was of old,
3.13.46: The image of the goddess we behold
3.13.47: Borne on the heads of maidens, and behind
3.13.48: The priestesses in beauteous rank you find.
3.13.49: An awful silence reigns: the goddess last
3.13.50: Approaches, and with her the pomp is past.
3.13.51: The dress was Greek, and such Halesus wore,
3.13.52: When in a fright he fled the Grecian shore;
3.13.53: His father kill'd, an Argive ship he fraught,
3.13.54: And to this coast the royal treasure brought.
3.13.55: Much peril had he past, much labour known,
3.13.56: O'er lands and seas, before he reach'd our own,
3.13.57: And landing built, with happy hand, the town,
3.13.58: Where first he did this festival revive,
3.13.59: And its Greek rules to the Phaliscans give;
3.13.60: The rites and sacrifices first he show'd,
3.13.61: As practis'd now within this ancient wood.
3.13.62: Ah, may these rites to all propitious be,
3.13.63: No more to those that serv'd them than to me.

3.14.1: I do not ask you would to me prove true,
3.14.2: Since you're a woman, and a fair one too.
3.14.3: Act what you please, yet study to disguise
3.14.4: The wanton scenes from my deluded eyes.
3.14.6: That crime which your confession would make great.
3.14.7: And 'twere unwise to trust the tell-tale light,
3.14.8: With the dark secrets of the silent night.
3.14.9: Tho' bought to be enjoy'd, a common whore
3.14.10: Ere she begins will shut the chamber door:
3.14.11: And will you turn debauch'd, then vainly own
3.14.12: How lewd you are, to this malicious town?
3.14.13: At least seem virtuous, and tho' false you be,
3.14.14: Say you are honest, and I'll credit thee.
3.14.15: Conceal your actions, and while I am by,
3.14.16: Let modest words your looser thoughts belie;
3.14.17: When to your private chamber you retire,
3.14.18: Unmask your lust, and vent each warm desire;
3.14.19: Throw off affected coyness, and remove
3.14.20: The bold intruder between thee and love:
3.14.21: Talk not of honour, lay that toy aside,
3.14.22: In men 'tis folly, and in women pride;
3.14.23: There without blushes you may naked lie,
3.14.24: Clasping his body with your tender thigh;
3.14.25: Shoot your moist dart into his mouth, to show
3.14.26: The sense you have of what he acts below;
3.14.27: Try all the ways, your pliant bodies twine,
3.14.28: In folds more strange than those of Aretine:
3.14.29: With melting looks fierce joys you may excite,
3.14.30: And with thick dying accents urge delight.
3.14.31: But when you're dress'd, then look as innocent
3.14.32: As if you knew not what such matters meant;
3.14.33: Cozen the prying town, and put a cheat
3.14.34: On it and me, I'll favour the deceit.
3.14.35: False as thou art, why must I daily see
3.14.36: Th' intriguing billet-doux he sends to thee?
3.14.37: The wanton sonnet, or soft elegy?
3.14.38: Why does your bed all tumbled seem to say,
3.14.39: See what they've done, see where the lovers lay!
3.14.40: Why do your locks and rumpled head-clothes show
3.14.41: 'Tis more than usual sleep that made 'em so?
3.14.42: Why are the kisses which he gave, betray'd
3.14.43: By the impression which his teeth had made?
3.14.44: Yet say you're chaste, and I'll be still deceived;
3.14.45: What much is wish'd for, is with ease believ'd.
3.14.46: But when you own what a lewd wretch thou art,
3.14.47: My blood grows cold and freezes at my heart,
3.14.48: Then do I curse thee, and thy crimes reprove,
3.14.49: But curse in vain, for still I find I love;
3.14.50: "Since she is false," oft to myself I cry,
3.14.51: "Would I were dead,"-yet 'tis with thee I'd die
3.14.52: I will not see your maid, to let me know
3.14.53: Who visits you, where, and with whom you go;
3.14.54: Nor by your lodging send my boy to scout,
3.14.55: And bring me word who passes in and out.
3.14.56: Enjoy the pleasure of the present times,
3.14.57: But let not me be knowing of your crimes.
3.14.58: Do you forswear't, tho' in the act you're caught,
3.14.59: I'll trust the oath, and think my eyes in fault.

3.15.1: To Virgil Mantua owes immortal fame,
3.15.2: Catullus to Verona gives a name;
3.15.3: Why mayn't, if I attempt some great design,
3.15.4: Peligne be as much oblig'd to mine?
3.15.5: Why mayn't my muse a glorious toil pursue,
3.15.6: And as much honour to my country do?
3.15.7: A people, who, when Rome has been alarm'd
3.15.8: By foreign foes, in her defence have arm'd;
3.15.9: Beneath your golden banners I have fought
3.15.10: So long, your discipline so much have taught,
3.15.11: 'Tis time to give me a discharge, to prove
3.15.12: Some other, some more glorious theme than love
3.15.13: See Bacchus beckons me my voice to raise,
3.15.14: Of lofty deeds to sings, in lofty lays;
3.15.15: To mount my muse on some more generous horse,
3.15.16: And try her courage in some daring course.
3.15.18: I'll be no more concern'd with love or you;
3.15.19: But what I write my being shall survive,
3.15.20: And in his verse the poet ever live.

1.1: DEAR Ulysses, your Penelope sends this epistle to you, so slow in your return home; write not any answer, but come yourself. Troy is no more, that city so justly odious to the Grecian dames: scarcely were Priam and all his kingdom worth such a mighty stir. Oh, how I wish that the infamous adulterer, when he sailed for Lacedæmon with his fleet, had been swallowed up by the raging seas! I had not then lain cold in a solitary bed, nor thus forlorn complained of the tedious days; the pendulous web would not then have tired my tender hands, while by such means I sought to elude the lingering nights. How often has my apprehension magnified your dangers? Love is a passion full of anxiety and fear. I often fancied you to myself assaulted by furious Trojans; and on hearing the name of Hector always turned pale. If any one informed me that Antilochus had been slain by that hero, the fate of Antilochus proved the cause of fresh disquiet to me; or, if informed that Patroclus had fallen in counterfeit armour, I lamented that this stratagem should fail of success. Tlepolemus had stained the Lycian spear with his blood, my anxiety was renewed by the catastrophè of Tlepolemus. In fine, as often as any fell in the Grecian camp, my fond heart was chilled with icy fear. But the righteous gods had regard to my chaste flame; my husband lives, and Troy is reduced to ashes. The Grecian chiefs have returned; our altars smoke; and the spoils of the barbarians are offered up to our gods. The matrons present grateful gifts for the safe return of their husbands; they in their turn sing the fate of Troy, constrained to yield to their better fortune. The good old men and timorous maids are stricken with admiration; and the eager wife hangs upon her husband's tongue as he relates. Some, ordering a table to be brought, describe upon it the fierce battles in which they were engaged, and with a little wine trace out the whole of Troy. This way, they say, flowed Simois; here is the Sigæan field; here stood the lofty palace of old Priam. There was the tent of Achilles; yonder that of Ulysses; here mangled Hector frightened the foaming horses; for old Nestor related all to your son, whom I sent to enquire after you; and he again to me. He told me likewise, that Rhesus and Dolon had been slain; how the one was surprised in his sleep, the other betrayed by guile. You also, my dear husband, alas! too, too forgetful of your family at home, adventured to enter the Thracian camp by stratagem in the night, and, assisted by Diomedes alone, to kill so great a number of men. No doubt you were wonderfully cautious, and did not forget your Penelope before the dangerous attempt. My heart never ceased beating till I heard how you rode victorious through the army of your friends upon Thracian horses. But what does it avail me that Troy has fallen by your hands, and that the spot, where formerly its walls stood, is now a level plain, if I still continue forlorn as when Troy flourished, and my husband is absent never to return? Troy remains to me alone; to others it is destroyed, and the victorious inhabitant tills it with the captive ox.
1.2: Now corn grows where once Troy stood; and the ground, fattened by Phrygian blood, produces a rich crop that tempts the hand of the reaper. The half-buried bones of heroes are ploughed up by the crooked share; and rising grass covers the ruins of the houses. Though victorious, you are still absent; nor can I possibly know the cause of your long stay, or in what corner of the world my cruel Ulysses lurks. Whatever stranger touches upon these coasts, is sure to be teased with a thousand questions about you; and, when he departs, is charged with a letter to deliver to you, in whatever region of the world he may chance to see you. We sent to Pylos, the Neleian kingdom of old Nestor; but we thence received no account beside uncertain report. We sent likewise to Sparta; but Sparta, being equally ignorant of the truth, left us uncertain that lands you might be wandering over, or where you could make so long a stay. It would be better for me, if the walls of Troy were still standing. Alas! unstable and unhappy, I am offended at my own wishes. I should know in what part of the world you fought, and dread only the dangers of war; nor should I be without companions to join in my complaint. Now I know not what to fear most. I am apt to fancy you exposed to every kind of hazard, and find myself bewildered in a wide field of care. Whatever dangers arise either from sea or land, these I suspect may be the causes of so long a delay. While I thus fondly revolve these things within myself, your it is possible, are the slave of some foreign beauty (such is the inconstancy of man). Perhaps too you divert her by telling what a homely wife you have, who minds only the spindle and the distaff. But I may be deceived, and this imaginary crime may vanish into mere air and conceit; nor can I persuade myself, that, if free to return, you would be absent from me. My father Icarius urges me to leave this widowed state, and never ceases chiding me for my continued delays. Let him chide on; I am yours, and must be called yours; Penelope will ever remain the wife of Ulysses. He at length is softened by my piety and chaste prayers, and forbears to use his authority. A dissipated set of wooers from Dulichium, Samos, and lofty Zacynthos, teize me without intermission. They reign uncontrolled in your palace, and devour your wealth, our very life and support. Why should I mention Pisander, Polybus, ugly Medon, and covetous Eurymachus and Antinoüs, beside many others, who all in your absence live upon the means gained at the hazard of your life? Indigent Irus, and your goat-herd Melanthius, serve to finish your disgrace. We are only three in number, unable to defend ourselves; your wife weak and helpless, Laërtes an old man, and Telemachus a child. That beloved boy we were lately in danger of losing, as, against all our wills, he prepared to go in quest of you to Pylos. May the gods grant, that by the order of fate he may be appointed to close my eyes; to close also yours. The neat-herd, swine-herd, and aged nurse, all join in this prayer. Laërtes, now unfit for arms, is unable to maintain your right against such a crowd of enemies. Telemachus, it is true, if spared, will arrive at a more vigorous age; but at present he requires his father's protection. Nor can it be supposed that I am able to drive away this hostile crowd. Come therefore speedily, you who are our only defence and sanctuary! You have (whom Heaven preserve) a son, whose tender years should have been formed to his father's virtue and prudence. Think of Laertes, and that it is your duty to close his eyes; he now languishes on the verge of dissolution. Surely I, who, when you left me, was but a girl, when you return must appear old and decayed.

2.1:
O DEMOPHOÖN, Phyllis, your Thracian hostess, complains of your absence beyond the promised time. You engaged to drop anchor on our coast, when the moon should have completed her orb. Already she hath four times waned, four times renewed her full orb; and your Athenian ships do not yet stem the Thracian tide. If you reckon time in the minute manner we lovers do, this complaint will not appear to have come before its day. Hope forsook me slowly too: we are unwilling to believe what may be injurious; but now I feel it, and, in spite even of love and myself, must believe. Often have I lied to myself for your sake; often flattered myself that the raging south winds would drive hither your swelling sails. In my resentment I have cursed Theseus, imagining that he would not suffer you to depart; yet he perhaps was no cause of your stay. Sometimes I dreaded that, in making towards the shallows of Hebrus, your ship might have been swallowed up by the foaming deep. Oft before the altars with offerings of incense have I, in a suppliant manner, implored the gods for your safety, O perfidious man! Oft seeing the winds favorable, the heaven serene, and the sea calm; Surely,
said I to myself, if alive, he will come.
In fine, my indulgent love represented to me all the obstacles that might prevent a speedy return; and I became ingenious at finding out excuses for you. But still you linger: the gods whom you invoked have not restored you to me; nor, moved by a sense of my love, do you return. O Demophoön, you have given both your words and sails to the winds. Your sails, alas! have failed to bring you back, and your words were insincere. What have I done, unless perhaps I have loved you to excess? But surely this crime might have rather endeared me to you. My only fault is, to have loved and entertained you, faithless man: yet this fault with you ought to be a merit. Where is now your honor? where are your oaths, and plighted troth? where are the many gods who dwelt on your perjured tongue? Where is now your matrimonial vow of constancy, which was to me the pledge and security of my phasing conjugal hopes? You swore by the tempest-beaten main, which before you had often crossed, and on which you were again to hazard yourself; you swore too by your grandsire (if he also is not falsely called so) who soothes the boisterous waves; by Venus doubly armed with her torch and bow, too successful, alas! with both against me; by Juno, who presides over the marriage-bed, and the sacred mysteries of the torch-bearing goddess. If each of these wronged powers should be disposed to take vengeance for the dishonor of invoking them falsely, you alone would be insufficient for the deserved punishment.
Fool that I was! I even repaired your leaky ships, that you might have a trusty fleet wherein to desert me; I supplied you also with rowers to help forward your flight. Wretched beyond expression, to be thus wounded by my own darts! Alas! I foolishly gave credit to your deluding words, of which you have such command. I confided in your race and kindred gods; I trusted to your tears: are these too taught to dissemble? Yes; even they have their artifices, and often conspire to delude. In fine, I believed your false protestations. Why did you commit so many perjuries to gain credit with me, when unhappily I was too willing to trust you? Nor do I repent that I received you into my harbour and kingdom: this ought to have been the utmost bound of my indulgence. I am only ashamed of having crowned my hospiality with the present of my bed, and yielded myself up to your embraces. Oh! had the night preceding that fatal one been my last, Phyllis had died chaste and honest. I hoped the best, because I was conscious I deserved well of you. Hope, founded upon desert, is just and unblameable. Surely it is no mighty glory to deceive a credulous maid; my innocent simplicity merited a kind return.
2.2: You have by your flattering words deluded a woman, and one that loved you. May the gods grant that this may be your greatest boast! May you stand in the midst of the city among the posterity of Ægeus! May the statue of your father graced with inscriptions and trophies stand first! When the stories of Scyron and stern Procrustes shall be read, Sinis, and the Minotaur; Thebes brought under subjection, the Centaurs dispersed, and the dark palace of the infernal god alarmed, may thy hated image bear this inscription: This is he, who betrayed his innocent believing hostess.
2.3: Of all the mighty acts of your father, Ariadne deserted seems to please you most. You admire only in him what alone seems to want an excuse, and are the perfidious heir of your father's treachery. She (nor do I envy her) enjoys a better match, and rides in state, drawn by harnessed tigers. But the Thracian youths whom I scorned before, now shun my embraces, because I preferred a stranger to my own subjects. Some in derision say, Let her now repair to learned Athens; we will find another to rule over warlike Thrace: the end proves all things.
2.4: May heaven deny him success in every thing, who presumes to judge of actions by the event: for, were your vessels to plough the Thracian waves, I should still be said to have studied my own and my people is good. But alas! I have consulted neither. You think no more of my palace, nor will you ever again bathe your wearied limbs in the Thracian lake. Our parting scene still presents itself to my fancy: your fleet being in readiness to sail, you embraced me, and, falling upon my neck, oft repeated the long-breathed kisses: you mixed your tears with mine, and complained that the wind was favorable; then parting, cried, Be sure, Phyllis, to expect your Demophoön.
2.5: Can I expect one who left me never to return? Can I expect ships never designed to visit these coasts? And yet I still expect you; return, though late, that your only crime may be too long a stay.
2.103: Unhappy Phyllis, what do you pray for? He perhaps is detained by another mistress, and a love that banishes all remembrance of thee. Alas! I fear that, since you left me, you have never once thought of Phyllis. Cruel fate! should you be at a loss to know who I Phyllis am, and whence; I: who admitted you, after a long course of wandering, into our Thracian harbours, and entertained you in so hospitable a manner; who increased your wealth from my own stock, supplied your wants by many gifts, and intended to have enriched you still more; who subjected to your rule the spacious kingdom of Lycurgus, too warlike and fierce to be awed by a female name; even from Rhodope covered with eternal snow, to shady Hæmus, and where gentle Hebrus rolls his sacred stream; on whom in an unlucky hour I bestowed my virgin love, and whom I suffered with treacherous hands to untie my chaste girdle. Doubtless Tisiphone howled over us in that fatal night, and the wandering owl complained in mournful notes. Alecto too was present, her hair wreathed with curling snakes; and lighted the tapers with infernal flame. Disconsolate, I tread the rocks and shore overgrown with shrubs, where-ever the wide sea lies open to my eyes. Whether by day, when earth relenting feels the genial heat, or by night when the stars shine, and cold damps fall, I am anxious in observing the course of the winds. If by chance I can espy and distant sail, forthwith I divine it to be my Demophoön. I run towards the shore whither the inconstant billows flow, and can scarcely be restrained even by the waves. The nearer they approach, the more my fears increase, till at last fainting away I am carried home by my train. Near my present abode is a bay, bent in the manner of a bow, whose sides running out into the sea form a precipice of rocks. Hence my despair has often urged me to throw myself headlong into the raging flood; and I am still resolved upon it, because you continue to deceive me. The friendly waves may perhaps waft me over to the Athenian shore, and my unburied remains may there meet your unexpecting eyes. Though more hard-hearted than iron or adamant, year even than yourself, you will in pity say; Alas! Phyllis, you ought not to have followed me thus. Oft I thirst after poisons; oft resolve to pierce my heart, and perish by a bloody death. Sometimes I think of tying a silken knot upon that neck, round which you have so often twined your treacherous arms. It is fixed; I must repair my ruined honor by a speedy death: when the mind is once determined, it is easy to choose the mode of dying. You shall be marked upon my tomb as the cruel cause of my death, and handed down to posterity in these or similar lines: Phyilis died by the cruelty of Demophoön; a faithful mistress by a perfidious guest. He was the barbarous cause; she herself gave the fatal blow.

3.1: THE letter which you now read in broken Greek, written by a foreign hand, comes from captive Briseis. Whatever blots you observe, were occasioned by my tears; but even tears are often more prevalent than words. If it may be allowed to complain a little of my lord and husband, I have a few causes of complaint against you, who are both. I do not blame you that I was so tamely delivered up to the king when demanded; and yet, even in that point, you are not altogether without blame: for no sooner was I demanded by Eurybates and Talthybius, than I was delivered up to be carried away by those military heralds. each regarding the other with a look of surprise, inquired in whispers, Where is their so famed love? I might have been detained somewhat longer; delay of miscry would have been grateful. Alas! when torn from you, I gave no parting kisses: but my tears flowed without ceasing; I tore my hair, and hapless seemed to myself, for the second time, a captive. I have often thought to deceive my keeper and escape, but trembled at the apprehension of falling into the hands of the enemy. I dreaded that, upon leaving the Grecian camp, I might again perhaps become a captive, and presented to some of the daughters-in-law of Priam. But I was delivered up, because so it must be. Though absent many nights, I am not demanded back. You linger, and are slow of resenting. Patroclus himself, when I was carried away, whispered in my ear, Why do you weep? your stay with Agamemnon will be very short. But your neglect of requiring me again from the hing is the least part of your crime; you even strive against my return. Weight now with yourself what right you have to the name of a lover. The sons of Telamon and Amyntor came ambassadors from Agamemnon; the first related to you by blood, the other your friend and
3.27: guardian: the son also of Laertes came; by whom I might have returned attended. Softening entreaties were added to their costly presents,—twenty shining vessels curiously wrought in Corinthian brass, and seven tripods, alike in weight and workmanship. To these were added twice five talents of gold, and twelve spirited steeds. matchless in the race; and (what might have well been spared) Lesbian girls of exquisite beauty, captives of that pillaged island. With these (but what need of this?) you had the choice of one of Agamemnon's three daughters for a wife. You refused to accept me with gifts, which, had Agamemnon consented to my ransom, you ought with joy to have carried to him. What have I done thus to merit your neglect, Achilles? Whither has your changeable love so soon fled? Does cruel fortune incessantly pursue the wretched? Shall no propitious gales favour my chaste hopes?
3.45: I saw the walls of Lyrnessus give way to your irresistible attack; nor was I an inconsiderable part of my native country. I saw three fall, brethren in blood as well as fate; who all sprang from the same mother. I saw my husband too stretched upon the bloody plain, and tossing with anguish his breast drenched in gore. Yet all these losses were recompensed in you alone; you were to me instead of a husband, a lord, a brother. You swore to me by the sacred deity of your sea-green mother, that it should be my happiness to have fallen a captive into your hands: for instance; to refuse me though offered to you with a large dowry, and reject the riches which you are urged to accept with me! It is even reported, that when returning Aurora gilds the mountains, you will open your flaxen sails to the cloud-bearing south winds. Soon as this cruel resolve reached my trembling ears, the blood forsook my breast; I was without life or soul. You will then abandon me! O barbarous man, what misery are you preparing for hapless Briseis! What solace can I expect in my forlorn state? Sooner may the gaping earth swallow me up, or the missile bolts of Jove overwhelm me, than I, abandoned, be doomed to behold the sea foaming after your Thessalian oars, and your ships deserting my distracted view. If you are determined to return, and visit again your native fields, I can be no very cumbersome load to your fleet. I submit to follow you as a captive subject to her conqueror, not as a spouse accompanying her husband. My hand will not disdain the meanest office. May the fairest of the Grecian dames become the happy partner of your bed, one worthy of such a father-in-law as the grandson of Jupiter and Ægina, to whom old Nereus will not disdain to be related. I her humble handmaid will diligently ply my task, and the twisted threads shall lessen the loaded distaff. Grant only that your wife, who I fear will regard me as a rival, be not suffered to treat me cruelly. Let her not tear my hair in your presence, while you unconcerned say, This girl was once dear to me. But I will submit to bear even this, rather than be left behind helpless and neglected. The dread of such treatment shakes my wretched frame. What can you wish for more? Agamemnon repents of his anger; and disconsolate Greece falls at your feet. You
3.75: who are conqueror every where else, be master also of yourself and your passions. Why is insulting Hector allowed to triumph over the Grecian troops?
